## Discussion

By re-analyzing reads typically discarded by transcriptomic pipelines, we show that cutaneous HPV is active in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) and quiet in healthy skin. In cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) and actinic keratosis, it appears only as a trace amount, a presence that increased sequencing depth or improved library chemistry cannot turn into a productive infection.

Previous studies have reported transcriptional silence of HPV in cutaneous carcinoma across four independent RNA-sequencing cohorts [@arron2011; @hultin2019; @arroyomuhr2021; @vandiver2021]. In situ hybridization in similar cohort sizes supports these findings [@fujimoto2019]. Because two prior series reached median depths of 35 and 66 million reads, shallow sequencing does not explain the negative results. Our study adds rigorous controls, a clear denominator, and a defined metric. While past work evaluated 11 to 345 specimens, we jointly analyze `r comma(stats$neo_n)` cSCC/AK libraries and `r comma(stats$uns_n)` unselected-skin libraries in one pipeline. This changes a simple absence report into a quantified case-control comparison with an effect size. Instead of only scoring viral presence or transcription, we measure productive replication against a calibrated baseline. We anchor this baseline using lesions with confirmed productive infection. We evaluate "no productive infection in cSCC/AK" using an instrument that reports `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% productivity in warts.

This result does not settle the underlying mechanism. All three models predict a declining viral signal along the progression axis. The hit-and-run model works because the virus becomes dispensable. Protective immunity works because virus-positive cells face negative selection [@strickley2019; @son2025]. Cis-restriction works because quiescence is the viral default [@rehm2022]. Our data measure this exact axis and cannot separate the three. Son and colleagues found elevated beta-HPV activity in sun-exposed skin. This finding does not conflict with our quiet reservoir. Their study observed local activity in keratinocyte clones. Our study used whole biopsies without sorting for ultraviolet exposure. A wide biopsy average dilutes a small clonal signal. The same logic applies to the HPV8-driven expansion of Lrig1⁺ follicular stem cells in actinic keratosis [@morgan2024]. We agree on viral presence, as we recovered trace HPV from `r pp(stats$ak_pctany)`% of AK libraries. An E6-driven stem cell mechanism requires oncogene function, not capsid production. This matches our non-productive footprint. A randomized trial shows that the nine-valent vaccine reduces the burden of actinic keratosis [@wenande2025]. This vaccine targets mucosal alpha types rather than the resident beta reservoir. Therefore, any protective effect likely depends on cross-reactive or non-specific immunity.

The rare productive infections we do find are beta-HPV, which constrains how the trace result should be read. Outside warts and EV, three primary-skin lesions carry unambiguous productive infection: an HPV12-productive cSCC, and two actinic-keratosis/cSCC libraries co-infected with HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. These are Betapapillomavirus 1, 5 and 2 respectively, so the genus running a complete productive program in these lesions is the same genus the cofactor debate concerns. Productive beta-HPV infection of primary skin is therefore possible and simply rare. The silence we report in cutaneous neoplasia is consequently not a ceiling on what beta-HPV can do in skin, because the same assay detects it doing exactly that in a handful of libraries. We are not aware of productive HPV12, HPV96 or HPV182 being reported from public RNA-seq of primary skin before.

A 2–4% active transcription rate does not contradict a 90% viral DNA reservoir. Three factors reconcile this gap. First, beta-HPV DNA loads sit below one copy per 60 cells [@weissenborn2012], falling beneath the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. Second, the tissue sources differ: skin epidemiology studies test surface swabs and hair bulbs (92% and 73% prevalence) [@rollison2019sites], while RNA-seq uses deep biopsies that miss surface and hair follicle layers. Third, screening panels miss 229 skin types that lack reference genomes [@bzhalava2014]. Ultimately, our figure reflects the actively transcribed portion of a widespread reservoir. DNA data confirms that the general reservoir differs from tumor-driving viruses: fewer than 5% of skin types match later cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) [@rollison2021], and paired eyebrow hair and cSCC showed only 9.1% genotype concordance in another cohort [@oh2026].

Unadjusted analyses are heavily dominated by contamination. For instance, cultured materials show a five-fold enrichment that reflects known HeLa cell contamination in archives [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], traced in one facility to a quality-control cell pool run with tumors [@selitsky2020]. Furthermore, over 65% of viral sequences from 712 libraries group with reagents or protocols instead of actual specimens [@asplund2019], and re-analyses have completely invalidated major archive-scale microbial findings [@gihawi2023]. While our safeguards are not individually new [@cantalupo2019], our contribution lies in operationalizing them by quantifying the size of each artifact rather than merely asserting it.

While petabase-scale surveys are now the standard method for establishing viral presence across body sites, a presence catalog cannot measure biological activity. Because these surveys rely on sequence assembly, integrated genomes fail to assemble across the virus-host junction. Consequently, the viral genome state must be inferred from individual reads or transcription rather than catalog membership alone. For example, conditioning data on near-complete L1-anchored contigs yields an intact E2 gene in 99.3% of cervical carcinoma contigs compared to 99.9% in skin (@supptbl-e2). This finding approaches a tautology, as the completeness criterion itself inherently selects for episomal genomes in both tissues.

Several limitations affect these findings, starting with the non-random nature of archival sampling, which makes the absolute healthy-skin rate an estimate. Furthermore, sequencing chemistry could only be resolved for `r pp(stats$chem_pct)`% of libraries, while input amount, RNA integrity, and fragment selection are entirely unrecoverable from the archived metadata. Additionally, bulk sequencing averages data across an entire biopsy, which dilutes focal transcription. This dilution is a documented reality for cutaneous HPV [@purdie2005] and means our productivity estimates represent a conservative lower bound. Finally, because tissue and diagnosis labels are programmatic and imperfect, viral typing is constrained by the reference panel, and the data are cross-sectional, these results describe productive-status phenomenology rather than prove a definitive mechanism.

Ultimately, cutaneous HPV presents a active, productive infection in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis, but leaves only a trace, non-productive footprint in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, regardless of sequencing depth or library chemistry. This distinct phenotype forms the fundamental baseline that any current theory of beta-HPV in skin cancer must address. Because all major hypotheses predict this exact outcome, simply measuring viral activity with higher precision will not differentiate between them. Instead, distinguishing these mechanisms will require study designs that disrupt this shared prediction. Crucial approaches include matched DNA and RNA profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, precise spatial resolution of residual viral particles relative to mutant clones and infiltrating T cells, and ongoing interventional studies. While single-cell resolution has already been demonstrated in cutaneous lesions [@devitt2019], the critical next step is applying this technology at a cohort scale across the actinic-keratosis-to-carcinoma transition.
